title: The Seminar That Changed Its Mind · 独立口语迁移
instructions: 先完成示范段的跟读诊断，再用不同人物、信息或立场录制自己的完整回答。示范与自由回答分别取证，服务未提供完整听音评阅时保持待评。
reference: Last Tuesday, the research seminar in Room 204 met to discuss a small study on study habits. The group had collected data for six weeks. Their hypothesis was simple: students who study in short, frequent sessions remember more than students who study in one long session. The seminar leader, Dr. Chen, asked the group to look at the results carefully. The first finding surprised everyone. The short-session group did better on a weekly quiz, but the long-session group did better on a final test. "That is not what we expected," said Marco, a second-year student. "Our hypothesis predicted one clear winner." The group checked the data again. The numbers were correct. The result was real, but it was not simple. This mixed pattern suggested that the two types of study might support different kinds of memory or performance. For example, short sessions may help students recall specific facts quickly, while longer sessions may allow deeper processing of complex ideas.
prompt:
Part 1
Do you often study in short sessions or long sessions?
What time of day do you usually study?
Do you take breaks when you study?
Have you ever changed your mind after seeing new information?

Part 2
Describe a time when you changed your opinion after learning new facts. You should say: what your first opinion was; what new facts you learned; how you changed your opinion; and how you felt about the change.

Part 3
Why is it important to revise a hypothesis when data changes?
How can students control their study habits better?
Do you think short study sessions are always better? Why or why not?
What can teachers do when students get unexpected results?
